parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that the area A m² of the pen is given by A = 60x − 2x².
parts.working: Side parallel to wall = 60 − 2x, so A = x(60 − 2x) (B1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Express A in the form p − q(x − r)² and hence find the greatest possible area and the value of x that gives it.
parts.answer: A = 450 − 2(x − 15)²; greatest area 450 m² when x = 15

practice.stem: The function f is defined for all real x by f(x) = −2x² + 8x + c, where c is a constant.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Express f(x) in the form a(x + b)² + d, giving d in terms of c.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The line y = 3 is a tangent to the curve y = f(x). Find the value of c.
parts.working: The maximum value 8 + c equals 3 (M1), c = −5 (A1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: For this value of c, find the set of values of x for which f(x) > −15.

practice.stem: The function f is defined by f(x) = 2x² − 8x + 1 for x ≤ 1.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Express f(x) in the form a(x + b)² + c.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the range of f.
parts.working: f is decreasing for x ≤ 1, f(1) = −5 (B1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find an expression for f⁻¹(x) and state its domain.
parts.working: y = 2(x − 2)² − 7 so (x − 2)² = (y + 7)/2 (M1). x ≤ 1 so take the negative root: x = 2 − √((y + 7)/2) (A1). Domain x ≥ −5 (B1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Solve the equation x⁴ − 13x² + 36 = 0.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Solve the equation 2x − 7√x + 3 = 0.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Solve the equation x^(2/3) − 5x^(1/3) + 4 = 0.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the exact real solutions of the equation 3x² + 4 = 20/x².
parts.working: Multiply by x²: 3x⁴ + 4x² − 20 = 0 (M1). (3x² + 10)(x² − 2) = 0 (M1 A1). x² = −10/3 has no real solution; x = ±√2 (A1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Solve the equation (x² − 3x)² − 2(x² − 3x) − 8 = 0.
parts.working: Let u = x² − 3x: u² − 2u − 8 = 0 (M1), u = 4 or −2 (A1). x² − 3x − 4 = 0 gives x = 4 or −1 (A1). x² − 3x + 2 = 0 gives x = 1 or 2 (M1 A1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the set of values of the constant k for which the equation x − 4√x + k = 0 has two distinct real roots.
parts.working: Let u = √x (u ≥ 0): u² − 4u + k = 0 needs two distinct non-negative roots u (M1). Discriminant 16 − 4k > 0 gives k < 4 (A1). Sum of roots 4 > 0 and product k ≥ 0 (k = 0 gives u = 0 or 4, i.e. x = 0 or 16) (M1). 0 ≤ k < 4 (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Solve the equation when k = 3.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the coordinates of the points where the line y = x + 1 meets the curve y = x² − 3x + 4.

practice.stem: The line 2x + y = 9 meets the curve x² + xy = 8 at the points A and B.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the coordinates of A and B.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the exact length of AB.

practice.stem: The curve y = 2x² − 5x + 3 and the line y = 3 − x meet at the points P and Q.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the coordinates of P and Q.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the equation of the perpendicular bisector of PQ.
parts.working: Midpoint (1, 2) (B1). Gradient PQ = −1 so perpendicular gradient 1 (M1). y − 2 = x − 1, y = x + 1 (A1).

practice.stem: The line y = kx − 2 meets the curve y = x² + 2 at two points. The x-coordinate of one point is four times the x-coordinate of the other.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that the x-coordinates satisfy x² − kx + 4 = 0.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the two possible values of k.
parts.working: Roots r and 4r: product 4r² = 4 so r = ±1 (M1 A1). Sum 5r = k, k = ±5 (A1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: For the positive value of k, find the coordinates of the two points.

practice.stem: The curve C has equation xy = 12.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the coordinates of the points where the line x + 2y = 10 meets C.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the set of values of the constant c for which the line x + 2y = c meets C at two distinct points.

practice.stem: The curve C has equation y = x² − 2x − 8.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the coordinates of the points where C crosses the axes and the coordinates of its vertex. Describe the shape of C.
parts.answer: x-axis (−2, 0) and (4, 0); y-axis (0, −8); vertex (1, −9); U-shaped (minimum) parabola
parts.working: (x − 4)(x + 2) = 0 (M1), (−2, 0), (4, 0) (A1). (0, −8) (B1). (x − 1)² − 9 gives vertex (1, −9), U-shape since coefficient of x² positive (B1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Hence solve the inequality x² − 2x − 8 < 0.
parts.working: B1: the curve is below the x-axis between the roots.

practice.stem: The curve C has equation y = (3 − x)(x + 1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe a sketch of C, giving the coordinates of the points where it meets the axes and of its turning point.
parts.answer: ∩-shaped parabola; meets x-axis at (−1, 0) and (3, 0), y-axis at (0, 3); maximum point (1, 4)
parts.working: Roots −1 and 3 and y-intercept 3 (B1). Coefficient of x² is −1 so ∩-shape (B1). Vertex at x = 1, y = 2 × 2 = 4 (B1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the number of real solutions of the equation (3 − x)(x + 1) = k when (i) k = 5, (ii) k = 4, (iii) k = 0.
parts.working: Maximum value 4: line y = 5 above the curve, none (B1); y = 4 touches at the vertex, one (B1); y = 0 cuts twice (B1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: The independent random variables X and Y have distributions N(20, 9) and N(15, 16) respectively. State the distribution of X + Y.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find P(X + Y > 40).

parts.label: a
parts.text: The independent random variables X and Y have distributions N(30, 5²) and N(24, 3²). Find P(X < Y).

parts.label: a
parts.text: The independent random variables X and Y have E(X) = 10, Var(X) = 4, E(Y) = 6 and Var(Y) = 2.5. Find E(3X − 2Y) and Var(3X − 2Y).

parts.label: a
parts.text: The mass of an empty glass jar is normally distributed with mean 250 g and standard deviation 8 g. The mass of honey put into a jar is normally distributed with mean 500 g and standard deviation 12 g, independently of the jar. Find the probability that a filled jar has a total mass of more than 770 g.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The masses of adults using a lift are normally distributed with mean 72 kg and standard deviation 11 kg. The lift's safe load is 600 kg. Eight adults, chosen at random, enter the lift. Find the probability that their total mass exceeds the safe load.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The random variable X has the distribution N(12, 2²). X₁, X₂, …, X₅ are five independent observations of X. Find P(X₁ + X₂ + X₃ + X₄ + X₅ > 65).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find P(5X > 65) and explain why this differs from your answer to (a).
parts.working:
B1 5X ~ N(60, 100)
B1 1 − Φ(0.5) = 0.309
B1 5X multiplies one observation, so variance is 25 × 4; the sum of five independent values has variance 5 × 4

parts.label: a
parts.text: A delivery driver's routes are of two types. The time for a type A route is distributed N(35, 4²) minutes and the time for a type B route is distributed N(22, 3²) minutes. On one day the driver completes 2 type A routes and 3 type B routes, all times being independent. Find the probability that the total time for the five routes is more than 140 minutes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The random variable X has the distribution N(4, 0.5²). X₁, X₂, X₃ and X₄ are independent observations of X, and T = X₁ + X₂ + X₃ − 2X₄. Find the mean and variance of T.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find P(T < 3).

parts.label: a
parts.text: The random variable X has the distribution N(3, 1.5²) and Y = 2X + 5. State the distribution of Y and find P(Y > 15).
parts.working:
B1 mean 11
B1 variance 4 × 2.25 = 9
M1 z = 4/3
A1 0.0912

parts.label: a
parts.text: Zara's journey to university has three independent stages: walking to the bus stop takes N(12, 2²) minutes, waiting for the bus takes N(8, 3²) minutes and the bus ride takes N(25, 4²) minutes. Find the probability that her total journey time is less than 40 minutes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The lifetimes of brand A light bulbs are distributed N(1200, 150²) hours and those of brand B bulbs are distributed N(1100, 100²) hours. One bulb of each brand is chosen at random. Find the probability that the brand A bulb lasts longer than the brand B bulb.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Rods of type A have lengths distributed N(42, 1.5²) cm and rods of type B have lengths distributed N(20, 0.8²) cm. One rod of each type is chosen at random. Find the probability that the type A rod is more than twice as long as the type B rod.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The diameters of bolts are normally distributed with mean 9.8 mm and standard deviation 0.05 mm. The diameters of the holes in nuts are normally distributed with mean 10.0 mm and standard deviation 0.08 mm. A bolt fits a nut if the bolt's diameter is less than the hole's diameter. A bolt and a nut are chosen at random. Find the probability that the bolt fits the nut.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Bags of flour have masses distributed N(2.02, 0.03²) kg. Twelve bags are packed into a box whose mass is distributed N(1.5, 0.1²) kg. All masses are independent. Find the probability that the total mass of the full box is between 25.6 kg and 26.0 kg.
parts.working:
B1 mean 24.24 + 1.5 = 25.74
B1 variance 12 × 0.0009 + 0.01 = 0.0208
M1 standardise both limits: −0.971 and 1.803
M1 subtract Φ values
A1 0.798

parts.label: a
parts.text: In a 4 × 100 m relay the four runners' times, in seconds, are independent and distributed N(12.1, 0.2²), N(11.8, 0.15²), N(12.3, 0.25²) and N(11.9, 0.18²). Find the probability that the team's total time is less than 47.8 seconds.

parts.label: a
parts.text: July rainfall in Lahore is modelled as N(190, 45²) mm and July rainfall in Islamabad as N(270, 60²) mm, independently. Find the probability that in a particular July Islamabad's rainfall is more than 1.5 times Lahore's.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The midday temperature in a city in June, in °C, is distributed N(28, 4²). The temperature F in °F is given by F = 1.8C + 32. State the distribution of F.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the probability that the midday temperature exceeds 90 °F.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A household's daily electricity use, in kWh, is distributed N(14, 3²), independently from day to day. Electricity costs Rs 55 per kWh plus a fixed charge of Rs 100 per day. Find the mean and variance of the total cost for a week (7 days).
parts.working:
B1 daily cost 55X + 100: mean 870
B1 weekly mean 7 × 870 = 6090
B1 variance 7 × 55² × 9 = 190 575

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the probability that the weekly cost exceeds Rs 6500.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A machine fills bags labelled 1 kg with sugar. The mass in a bag is distributed N(1.008, 0.006²) kg. A shopkeeper buys 5 bags at random. Find the probability that the total mass of sugar in the 5 bags is less than 5 kg.

parts.label: a
parts.text: In a class, Physics marks are distributed N(58, 12²) and Chemistry marks N(62, 10²). Assuming a student's two marks are independent, find the probability that a randomly chosen student's Physics mark is at least 10 more than their Chemistry mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Comment on the independence assumption.
parts.answer: Unlikely to be true: a student good at one science is likely to do well in the other.
parts.working: B1 sensible comment that the marks are probably positively related

parts.label: a
parts.text: A river ferry carries 20 cars and 10 vans. The masses of cars are distributed N(1.4, 0.2²) tonnes and the masses of vans N(2.6, 0.3²) tonnes, all independently. The ferry's maximum safe load is 56 tonnes. Find the probability that the total mass of the vehicles exceeds the maximum safe load.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Sacks of basmati rice have masses distributed N(25.2, 0.4²) kg. A restaurant buys 4 sacks chosen at random. Find the probability that their total mass is within 0.5 kg of 100.8 kg.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Boxes have masses distributed N(15, 2²) kg independently. A trolley can safely carry 250 kg. Find the largest number of boxes, n, that can be loaded so that the probability that the total mass exceeds 250 kg is less than 0.05.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The independent random variables X and Y have distributions N(50, 4) and N(49, 5). Find P(|X − Y| < 3).

parts.label: a
parts.text: The masses of men in a town are distributed N(78, 10²) kg and the masses of women N(62, 8²) kg. Three men and four women are chosen at random. Find the probability that the total mass of the three men is greater than the total mass of the four women.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The independent random variables X and Y have distributions N(μ, 3²) and N(2μ, 4²). Given that P(X + Y > 60) = 0.0228, find μ.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The independent random variables X and Y have distributions N(10, σ²) and N(15, 9). Given that P(2X > Y) = 0.9, find σ.
parts.working:
B1 2X − Y has mean 5
B1 variance 4σ² + 9
M1 5/√(4σ² + 9) = 1.282
M1 4σ² + 9 = 15.22
A1 σ = 1.25

parts.label: a
parts.text: A wall is built from 12 courses of bricks. The height of each course is distributed N(7.5, 0.2²) cm and between consecutive courses there is a layer of mortar whose thickness is distributed N(1.0, 0.15²) cm. All heights are independent. Find the probability that the height of the wall is between 100 cm and 102.5 cm.
parts.working:
B1 11 layers of mortar; mean 90 + 11 = 101
B1 variance 12 × 0.04 + 11 × 0.0225 = 0.7275
M1 z values −1.172 and 1.759
M1 subtract Φ values
A1 0.840

parts.label: a
parts.text: In a garment factory, the numbers of shirts finished in an hour by machines A, B and C are modelled by independent normal distributions N(120, 9²), N(95, 7²) and N(30, 5²). Find the probability that in a given hour machine A finishes more shirts than machines B and C together.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a normal model for these counts is only an approximation.
parts.answer: The numbers of shirts are discrete (whole numbers), while the normal distribution is continuous.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Floor tiles have lengths distributed N(30, 0.4²) cm. A row of 10 tiles is laid with a fixed gap of 0.3 cm between neighbouring tiles. The row must fit along a wall of length 303.5 cm. Find the probability that a row of 10 randomly chosen tiles, with gaps, fits.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why it would be wrong to use 10X, where X is the length of one tile, for the total length of the tiles.
parts.answer: 10X assumes all ten tiles have the same length; the tiles vary independently, so the variance is 10 × 0.16, not 100 × 0.16.
parts.working: B1 independent tiles: add variances, not multiply one tile

parts.label: a
parts.text: A sector OAB of a circle has centre O, radius 12 cm and angle AOB = 0.85 radians. Find the length of the arc AB.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the area of the sector OAB.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Express 135° in radians, giving your answer as an exact multiple of π.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A sector of a circle of radius 8 cm has angle 135°. Find, in terms of π, the perimeter and the area of the sector.
parts.working: Arc = 8 × 3π/4 = 6π B1; perimeter = 8 + 8 + 6π = 16 + 6π B1; area = ½ × 64 × 3π/4 = 24π B1

parts.label: a
parts.text: A car windscreen wiper arm is pivoted at a point O. The rubber blade lies along the arm from 15 cm to 50 cm from O. In one sweep the arm turns through an angle of 2.1 radians. Find the area of windscreen cleaned in one sweep. Give your answer correct to 3 significant figures.
parts.working: Area = ½ × 50² × 2.1 − ½ × 15² × 2.1 M1 M1 (difference of two sectors); = 2388.75 ≈ 2390 cm² A1

parts.label: a
parts.text: A sector of a circle has radius 6 cm and area 45 cm². Find the angle of the sector in radians.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the perimeter of the sector.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A sector of a circle has arc length 14 cm and area 70 cm². Find the radius of the circle and the angle of the sector in radians.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A round pizza of diameter 30 cm is cut into slices from its centre. One slice is a sector with angle π/5 radians. Find, in terms of π, the length of the crust (the curved edge) of this slice.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find, in terms of π, the area of the top surface of this slice.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Ayesha cuts a second slice whose top surface area is 18π cm². Find the angle of this slice in radians.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A pendulum consists of a small bob on a light rod of length 80 cm. The bob swings from 0.3 radians on one side of the vertical to 0.3 radians on the other side. Find the distance travelled by the bob in one swing from one extreme position to the other.
parts.working: Angle turned = 0.6 rad B1; s = 80 × 0.6 = 48 cm B1

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find how much higher the bob is at an extreme position than at its lowest point. Give your answer correct to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The minute hand of the clock on a clock tower in Faisalabad is 1.8 m long. Find the angle, in radians, that the minute hand turns through in 20 minutes.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the distance moved by the tip of the minute hand in 20 minutes, correct to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the area swept out by the minute hand in 20 minutes, correct to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Points A and B lie on a circle with centre O and radius 5 cm, and angle AOB = 1.2 radians. Find the length of the chord AB.
parts.working: AB = 2 × 5 sin 0.6 (or cosine rule) M1; = 5.65 cm A1

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the area of the minor segment cut off by the chord AB.
parts.working: Sector = ½ × 25 × 1.2 = 15 B1; triangle = ½ × 25 sin 1.2 = 11.65 B1; segment = 15 − 11.65 = 3.35 cm² A1

parts.label: a
parts.text: A sector of a circle has angle 2 radians and perimeter 28 cm. Find the radius of the circle.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the area of the sector.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A sector OAB has centre O, radius 10 cm and angle AOB = θ radians. The perimeter of the sector is 32 cm. Find θ.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the area of the region bounded by the chord AB and the arc AB, correct to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: a
parts.text: In a park in Islamabad, a curved path is the region between two arcs with the same centre O. The inner arc has radius 7 m and the outer arc has radius 9 m, and both arcs subtend an angle of 1.5 radians at O. The two straight ends of the path lie along radii. Find the area of the path.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the total length of the boundary of the path.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Edging is fixed along the whole boundary at a cost of Rs 850 per metre. Find the total cost.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Points A and B lie on a circle with centre O and radius 8 cm. The chord AB has length 10 cm. Show that angle AOB = 1.350 radians, correct to 4 significant figures.
parts.working: sin(½AOB) = 5/8 M1; AOB = 2 sin⁻¹(0.625) = 1.3503 A1 (or cosine rule: cos AOB = (64 + 64 − 100)/128)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the area of the minor segment cut off by AB, correct to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The sector OAB has centre O, radius 5 cm and angle AOB = 0.9 radians. The tangent to the arc at A meets the line OB extended at T. Find the area of the region bounded by AT, TB and the arc AB, correct to 3 significant figures.
parts.working: AT = 5 tan 0.9 = 6.301 M1; triangle OAT = ½ × 5 × 6.301 = 15.75, sector = 11.25 M1; region = 4.50 cm² A1

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the perimeter of this region, correct to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A badge is made from an equilateral triangle ABC of side 4 cm. Each side is replaced by an arc of a circle centred at the opposite vertex (for example, arc BC has centre A and radius 4 cm). Find, in terms of π, the perimeter of the badge.
parts.working: Each arc = 4 × π/3 M1; total = 3 × 4π/3 = 4π A1

parts.label: b
parts.text: Show that the area of the badge is 8(π − √3) cm².
parts.working: Triangle area = ½ × 16 × sin(π/3) = 4√3 B1; each segment = ½ × 16 × π/3 − 4√3 = 8π/3 − 4√3 M1 A1; total = 4√3 + 3(8π/3 − 4√3) = 8π − 8√3 A1

parts.label: a
parts.text: A chord AB of a circle with centre O and radius 6 cm subtends an angle of 2π/3 radians at O. Find the exact area of the minor segment cut off by AB.
parts.working: Sector = ½ × 36 × 2π/3 = 12π B1; triangle = ½ × 36 × sin(2π/3) = 9√3 B1; segment = 12π − 9√3 A1

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the exact perimeter of the minor segment.
parts.working: Arc = 6 × 2π/3 = 4π B1; AB = 2 × 6 sin(π/3) = 6√3 M1; perimeter = 4π + 6√3 A1

parts.label: a
parts.text: OABC is a rhombus with sides of length 7 cm and angle AOC = 1.1 radians. An arc AC of a circle with centre O and radius 7 cm is drawn inside the rhombus. Find the area of the region inside the rhombus but outside the sector OAC, correct to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the perimeter of this region.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A sector of a circle has radius r cm and angle θ radians. The perimeter of the sector is equal to twice the length of its arc. Find θ.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The area of the sector is 36 cm². Find r and the perimeter of the sector.
parts.working: ½r² × 2 = 36 M1; r = 6 A1; perimeter = 12 + 12 = 24 cm A1

parts.label: a
parts.text: A circular garden in the middle of a roundabout in Lahore has centre O and radius 15 m. A straight footpath crosses the garden along a chord AB of length 24 m. Find angle AOB in radians, correct to 4 significant figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the area of the smaller of the two parts into which the path divides the garden, correct to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The sector OAB has centre O, radius 9 cm and angle AOB = 1.2 radians. The point C lies on OA with OC = 5 cm. Find the area of the region R bounded by the line segments CA and CB and the arc AB, correct to 3 significant figures.
parts.working: Sector = ½ × 81 × 1.2 = 48.6 B1; triangle OCB = ½ × 5 × 9 × sin 1.2 = 20.97 M1; R = 27.6 cm² A1

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the perimeter of R, correct to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Two circles intersect at A and B. The first has centre P and radius 6 cm; the second has centre Q and radius 8 cm, and PQ = 10 cm. Show that angle PAQ is a right angle, and find angles APB and AQB in radians, correct to 4 significant figures.
parts.working: 6² + 8² = 10² so PAQ = 90° (converse of Pythagoras) B1; cos APQ = 6/10 M1; APB = 2 cos⁻¹ 0.6 = 1.855 A1; AQB = 2 cos⁻¹ 0.8 = 1.287 A1

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the area of the region common to both circles, correct to 3 significant figures.
parts.working: Segment in circle P: ½ × 36(1.8546 − sin 1.8546) = 16.10 M1 A1; segment in circle Q: ½ × 64(1.2870 − sin 1.2870) = 10.46 M1; total = 26.6 cm² A1

parts.label: a
parts.text: A farmer in Sindh uses 24 m of fencing to enclose a sector-shaped pen of radius r m and angle θ radians. The fencing goes along both radii and the arc. Show that the area A m² of the pen is given by A = 12r − r².

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the maximum area of the pen and the value of θ for which it occurs.
parts.answer: Maximum area 36 m² when r = 6 and θ = 2
parts.working: dA/dr = 12 − 2r = 0 (or complete the square: 36 − (r − 6)²) M1; r = 6, A = 36 A1; θ = (24 − 12)/6 = 2 A1

parts.label: a
parts.text: Three pipes, each with a circular cross-section of radius 5 cm, are tied together so that each pipe touches the other two. Find the exact area of the cross-section of the gap enclosed between the three pipes.
parts.working: Centres form an equilateral triangle of side 10 B1; triangle area = ½ × 100 × sin(π/3) = 25√3 M1; three sectors of angle π/3: 3 × ½ × 25 × π/3 = 25π/2 M1; gap = 25√3 − 25π/2 A1

parts.label: b
parts.text: Hence give this area correct to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A sector OAB has centre O, radius 12 cm and angle AOB = π/3. A circle with centre C and radius r cm lies inside the sector and touches OA, OB and the arc AB. Show that OC = 2r and hence find r.
parts.working: C lies on the bisector of angle AOB, so the angle between OC and OA is π/6 B1; r = OC sin(π/6) so OC = 2r M1 A1; OC + r = 12 ⇒ 3r = 12, r = 4 A1

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find, in terms of π, the area of the part of the sector that lies outside the circle.
parts.working: Sector = ½ × 144 × π/3 = 24π; circle = 16π M1; 24π − 16π = 8π A1

parts.label: a
parts.text: Triangle ABC is isosceles with AB = AC = 10 cm and angle BAC = 0.8 radians. An arc BC is drawn with centre A and radius 10 cm. A semicircle is drawn on BC as diameter, on the side of BC away from A. Find the length of BC, correct to 4 significant figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the area of the region inside the semicircle but outside the sector ABC, correct to 3 significant figures.
parts.working: Semicircle = ½π(3.894)² = 23.82 M1 A1; segment of sector = ½ × 100(0.8 − sin 0.8) = 4.132 M1 A1; region = 23.82 − 4.13 = 19.7 cm² A1

parts.label: a
parts.text: ABCD is a square of side 8 cm. Two quarter circles of radius 8 cm are drawn inside the square, one with centre A passing through B and D, and one with centre C passing through B and D. Find, in terms of π, the perimeter of the leaf-shaped region that lies inside both quarter circles.
parts.working: Each arc = 8 × π/2 = 4π M1; perimeter = 8π A1

parts.label: b
parts.text: Show that the area of the leaf-shaped region is 32(π − 2) cm².
parts.working: Half the leaf = quarter circle − triangle ABD = 16π − 32 M1 A1; leaf = 2(16π − 32) = 32π − 64 = 32(π − 2) A1

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the percentage of the square that lies outside the leaf, correct to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: a
parts.text: In a rice mill, a tight belt passes around two pulleys with radii 9 cm and 4 cm. The centres of the pulleys are 13 cm apart. The straight parts of the belt are common external tangents to the two circles. Show that each straight part has length 12 cm.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Let α = sin⁻¹(5/13). Explain why the belt is in contact with the larger pulley over an angle of (π + 2α) radians, and find α correct to 4 significant figures.
parts.working: Radii to the tangent points are perpendicular to the straight parts, which make angle α with the line of centres where sin α = 5/13 M1; so the contact angle on the larger pulley is π + 2α (and on the smaller π − 2α) A1; α = 0.3948 B1

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the total length of the belt, correct to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A street vendor in Karachi makes paper cones for roasted chana. Each cone is made by joining the two straight edges of a sector of paper of radius 15 cm and angle θ radians, without overlap. The circular rim of the cone has radius 6 cm. Find θ, giving your answer as an exact multiple of π.
parts.working: Arc length = circumference of rim: 15θ = 2π × 6 M1; θ = 12π/15 = 4π/5 A1

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find, in terms of π, the area of paper used for each cone.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the volume of chana a full cone can hold, correct to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A circle has centre O and radius 5 cm. A point T is 13 cm from O, and the tangents from T touch the circle at A and B. Show that angle AOB = 2.352 radians, correct to 4 significant figures.
parts.working: OA ⟂ TA, so cos AOT = 5/13 M1; AOB = 2 cos⁻¹(5/13) = 2.3520 A1

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the area of the region bounded by TA, TB and the minor arc AB, correct to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the perimeter of this region, correct to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A window in a Mughal-style building is a rectangle 1.2 m wide and 1.5 m tall, topped by a pointed arch. The arch is formed by two arcs, each of radius 1.2 m. One arc has its centre at the top left corner of the rectangle and the other at the top right corner; the arcs meet at the top point P of the window. Explain why the centres of the arcs and P form an equilateral triangle, and show that the area of the arch region above the rectangle is (0.48π − 0.36√3) m².
parts.working: Each centre is 1.2 m from P and the centres are 1.2 m apart, so all sides are 1.2 m B1; each arc subtends π/3 at its centre B1; arch = 2 × ½ × 1.44 × π/3 − ½ × 1.44 × sin(π/3) M1; = 0.48π − 0.36√3 A1

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the total area of the window, correct to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the perimeter of the window, correct to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: a

parts.working: M1 binomial terms with n = 14, p = 0.3; A1 P(3) = 0.194; A1 P(4) = 0.229, P(5) = 0.196; A1 most likely value 4.

parts.label: a

parts.label: b

parts.working: M1 P(X > 4) = 1 − P(X ≤ 4); M1 at least 3 correct terms; A1 0.370.

parts.working: M1 P(X = 2) = 0.2966; M1 P(X ≥ 1) = 1 − 0.75⁶ = 0.8220; M1 conditional probability ratio; A1 0.361.

practice.stem: Sara and Hina play a squash match. The first player to win 3 games wins the match. Sara wins any game with probability 0.6, independently of other games.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the probability that Sara wins the match is equal to P(X ≥ 3), where X ~ B(5, 0.6), even though the match may finish before 5 games are played.
parts.answer: Imagine all 5 games played: Sara wins the match exactly when she wins at least 3 of them
parts.working: B1 extending to 5 games does not change the winner; B1 so Sara wins iff she wins ≥ 3 of 5.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the probability that Sara wins the match.

parts.working: M1 exactly 1 goal in first 4 attempts: 4 × 0.35 × 0.65³; M1 multiply by 0.35; A1 0.135.

parts.text: Show that the probability that the first success occurs on an odd-numbered trial is p/(1 − q²), where q = 1 − p.

practice.subtopic: Loss of kinetic energy in collisions

parts.label: a
parts.text: Particle A of mass 2 kg moving at 5 m s⁻¹ collides with a stationary particle B of mass 3 kg. After the collision A and B both move in the original direction of A, with speeds w m s⁻¹ and v m s⁻¹ respectively. The loss of kinetic energy is 14.4 J. Show that v² − 4v + 3.84 = 0.
parts.working:
M1 momentum: 10 = 2w + 3v
M1 energy: 25 − 14.4 = w² + 1.5v²
M1 substitute w = 5 − 1.5v
A1 3.75v² − 15v + 14.4 = 0 → v² − 4v + 3.84 = 0 (AG)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Hence find v and w, explaining why one solution must be rejected.
parts.working:
M1 v = 2.4 or 1.6
A1 v = 1.6 gives w = 2.6 > v, so A would pass through B: reject
A1 v = 2.4, w = 1.4

practice.subtopic: Loss of kinetic energy in collisions

parts.label: a
parts.text: Particle A of mass 1 kg moving at 6 m s⁻¹ collides with stationary particle B of mass 2 kg. After the collision A rebounds with speed 2 m s⁻¹ and B moves at 4 m s⁻¹. Show that momentum is conserved and that no kinetic energy is lost.
parts.working:
B1 momentum 6 before, −2 + 8 = 6 after
M1 KE before 18 J, after 2 + 16
A1 equal, so no loss

parts.label: b
parts.text: B then collides with a stationary particle C of mass m kg and they coalesce. The loss of kinetic energy in this collision is 12 J. Find m.
parts.working:
M1 common speed 8/(2 + m)
M1 KE after = 32/(2 + m)
M1 16 − 32/(2 + m) = 12
A1 m = 6
